title: Who are you
hook: the yogis ask Nanak his name, his path, where he comes from and where he goes

segments.voice: Yesterday the Sidh Gosht opened: the yogis sat down, Nanak bowed to the One. Your line was a conversation. Did you let someone finish their whole question? Today they ask theirs. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

Name. Place of residence. Purpose of visit. Final destination. A passport desk wants four answers, and it wants them short. The yogis in the Sidh Gosht ask a stranger almost the same list. Who are you? What's your name? What path are you on, and what are you after? Where do you sit, where do you stay, where did you come from, and where are you going? They ask him, in paraphrase, to answer truthfully. It's a fair set of questions for a guest who has just walked into their circle. Today: who are you, and the strange, exact answer Nanak gives.
screen: `NAME. PATH. PURPOSE.` → `WHERE FROM? WHERE TO?` → `THE YOGIS ASK THE GUEST.`

segments.voice: Listen to what Nanak leaves out. No village. No family name. No caste, no sect, no teacher's lineage, none of the things a stranger would normally use to place him. Here's his answer, in paraphrase. The One lives deep in every heart, and that is where I sit and where I stay. I walk in the will of the True Guru. I came in the ease of the divine order, and I go wherever that order sends me. Nanak lives forever under that will. My seat is the One who does not move; that's what the Guru's teaching gave me. And the one who turns toward the Guru comes to understand, recognizes their own self, and merges into the True. Turn that over. They asked where he sits, and he names a seat inside every heart. They asked where he comes from and where he's going, and he doesn't give a road; he gives a direction, the hukam, the order that sends him. They asked his path, and he says, more or less, I walk where I'm told. That isn't dodging. It's answering one level down. A name tells you what to call someone. A hometown tells you where they started. Nanak's answer tells you what he's oriented toward, which is the one thing about a person a name never says. And there's a quiet phrase near the end: aap pachhaanai, a person recognizes their own self. In this poem, knowing who you are isn't the starting point you hand over at the desk. It's something reached, by turning toward the Guru. So the yogis' question turns out to be the right one. Who are you? It's just bigger than they thought, and the answer isn't on a passport. That's today's line.
screen: `NO VILLAGE, NO CASTE, NO LINEAGE.` · `MY SEAT IS IN EVERY HEART.` · `I GO WHERE THE ORDER SENDS ME.` · `KNOWING YOURSELF IS REACHED.` · then, large: `WHO ARE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer who you are in one line. Let the breath settle first. Then let the usual answers come up and pass by: your name, your job, your town, the role you play at home. They're all true; just set them down for a moment. Ask the question again underneath them. Who are you, if you answer the way Nanak did, by what you're turned toward? Don't hurry. When a line comes, even a clumsy one, hold it for a few breaths. You don't have to tell anyone. If you pray, you can set your line down under the hukam, the order Nanak said he walks in. The bell holds the time.
Who are you. The yogis' first question to Nanak, answered not with a name or a town but with a seat in every heart and a life lived under the divine order. Today's word.
Your line: who are you. The next time someone asks what you do, give the usual answer, and then quietly answer the bigger question for yourself. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: In katha on the Sidh Gosht, teachers often linger on this exchange, and Sikhs hear in Guru Nanak's answer the idea of living under hukam, the divine order, rather than defining oneself by caste or lineage.
